Entries.Text: Collision
Collision Editor
This tool isn't supported for this game. Dark Souls II (the original release) isn't supported because its Havok 2012 collision can't be written; use Scholar of the First Sin.

Cleanup isn't available for Demon's Souls, Dark Souls, Dark Souls Remastered and Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin. Their collision files are named by model and area, which the unused check doesn't read.

Reshape, create and add walls to map collision. Edit moves the vertices of the displayed collision; Create adds a new collision to the active map, with its high, low and fall protection files; Cleanup removes collision files that no part uses.

1. Choose the Layer to edit (show it if it is hidden), then click Start Collision Edit.
2. Pick a Brush mode (Raise, Lower, Drag or Smooth) and its Radius. Move the mouse over the collision: the sphere shows the brush's reach, and the Cursor section shows how many vertices it covers.
3. Hold the left mouse button to brush. While held, Raise, Lower and Smooth apply again at each interval wherever the brush is; Drag slides the vertices under the brush with the mouse at their height. With Link High and Low on, the other layer follows.
4. Commit (above the tabs) rebuilds the edited files and writes them into the project; Discard restores the vertices.

1. Check the Map: the collision is made for the active map.
2. Choose the Collision Types to make: any or all of High, Low and Fall Protection. Fall Protection builds walls along the mesh's outer edges, with the options shown under it (Elden Ring, Nightreign, Armored Core VI and The Duskbloods (Network Test) only).
3. Choose a Shape: a basic shape (made at the placement orb), the FLVERs of the selected map pieces and assets, or User-Defined points placed in the viewport. Set its Facing, Material and size.
4. Keep the suggested Model ID, or type one. An ID the map already uses overwrites that collision after you confirm.
5. Create writes the new files into the project and adds a part that places them (saved with the map). The button under the result selects it.
Glossary
The collision terms the tool uses.
Layers (high, low, fall protection)

A collision model has up to three layers, each in its own file. High (h) and low (l) are the same ground at two levels of detail, with h more detailed. Fall protection (f) is a set of thin walls along edges. Each layer is drawn and edited separately.
Collision files
Named for the layer, map and model: h10_00_00_00_002400.hkx.dcx is the high collision of model h002400 in m10_00_00_00, and l... and f... are its other layers.
Binder
The archive that holds every file of one layer of a map (its h, l or f files). Committing, creating or generating writes the whole binder into the project.
Body
A shape inside a collision file. An h or l file holds one body, a compressed mesh of triangles; an f file holds one body per run of wall.
Model and collision part

A model is a collision's mesh, identified by h and six digits (h002400). A collision part is the map entry that places a model. Several parts can place one model and all show its mesh, so an edit changes every one.
Linked layers
High and low don't share vertices. With Link High and Low on, editing one moves the other's vertices near the edit: fully within the link distance, and fading out beyond it across the radius.
Radius

How far around the brush's centre a stroke reaches, shown by the brush sphere. Vertices nearer the centre move more; vertices past the radius don't move. If no vertex is inside the brush, only the nearest corner of the triangle under it moves.
Facing
Which side of a triangle is solid. Ground faces up. If a new collision can be fallen or walked through in game, try the other facing.
Collision material

The material of each triangle, picked by name. A FLVER mesh whose material is named hkm_Name_Property keeps that material. The Material tab shows each face's material in its own colour, and paints new ones.
Placement orb
The marker in front of the camera where new objects are placed (viewport Settings > Placement Orb). Basic shapes are created there, and the first Gizmo point is spawned there.
Fall protection

Thin vertical walls that stop falls off the edges of collision. The game doesn't protect every drop, and its walls follow the walkable edge rather than the collision's edge, so generated walls are a starting point.
Drop edges
Outer edges of standable ground with nothing, or ground well below, just past them. Drop Edges Only adds walls to these edges only, leaving out open seams between pieces of floor.
Collision filter
A value on each fall protection body. The game's walls use 0 or 1. Copy the value of the map's other walls.
Commit and saving

Moved vertices are a preview until committed. Commit, Create and Generate write their files into the project immediately. Their undo and redo show in the viewport at once and reach the files when the map is saved; a created part is saved with the map.
Viewport
Whether collision is drawn, what the viewport's clicks, keys and gizmo do, and any uncommitted edits. Shown on every tab.
Show Collision

The viewport's collision filter, as in the Filters menu. Collision must be shown to edit it and to see the previews. Which layers (high, low, fall protection) are drawn is set separately; the Edit tab offers to show the layer it edits.
Clicks in the viewport select map objects as usual.

Actions
Start or stop editing. Commit and Discard are above the tabs, shown while there are edits.
Start Collision Edit

Show the brush on the collision under the mouse, so you can move its vertices by holding the left mouse button. While editing, clicks in the viewport brush instead of selecting. This turns off the Navigation tool's vertex editing, which uses the same keys. Editing stops when you leave this tab or close the Collision Editor; uncommitted edits are kept, and Commit and Discard appear above the tabs.
Stop Collision Edit
Hide the cursor. Uncommitted edits are kept, and you can commit or discard them later.
Commit Changes

Rebuild the edited collision from the moved vertices and write its collision binders into the project immediately. You can undo this: the undo shows in the viewport at once and reaches the project's files when the map is saved.
Discard Changes
Restore every moved vertex to its original position.
Layer
The collision layer the cursor edits. Only this layer is hit, because the layers overlap.
High and low collision are the same ground at two levels of detail. Fall protection is a separate barrier.
{0} collision isn't displayed, so the cursor can't be placed on it.
Display {0} Collision
Display this collision layer for every collision part.
Linked Layers
Whether a part's other layer follows the edits, so high and low collision stay on the same ground.
Link High and Low

Move the other layer's vertices under the brush along with the edited layer (Smooth flattens each layer towards its own plane), and commit both files. The layers don't share vertices or always cover the same ground, so only vertices within the link distance follow. Works whether or not the other layer is displayed.
{0} collision isn't linked to another layer.
{0} collision follows edits to {1} collision.
Link Distance
How close the other layer's vertices must be to the brush's centre to follow it fully. Beyond this, the radius fades them out.
The distance in world units. Most low vertices are within 0.5 of the high collision; larger distances may pull in nearby surfaces that aren't the same ground.
Linked: {0}, {1} of its vertices follow.
Linked: {0}, but none of its vertices are within the link distance, so it doesn't follow here.
A stroke here moves {0} vertices in {1} files (radius {2}).
Brush centre: {0}
Cursor Display
The opacity of the brush sphere (its size is the Radius). Rarely changed, so hidden by default.
Brush
What holding the left mouse button does to the vertices under the brush. The mode keys switch it between strokes.
The brush mode. Raise, Lower and Smooth apply at each interval while the button is held; Drag follows the mouse.
Raise
Raise: lift the vertices under the brush by the step at each interval while the button is held, most at the centre.
Lower
Lower: sink the vertices under the brush by the step at each interval while the button is held, most at the centre.
Drag
Drag: grab the vertices under the brush when the button is pressed, and slide them with the mouse at their height until it is released.
Smooth
Smooth: pull the vertices under the brush towards their best-fit plane at each interval while the button is held. Bumps flatten; slopes, ramps and walls keep their angle.
Strength
How far towards the plane the vertices at the brush's centre move each interval. Vertices further out move less.
100% puts the centre vertices on the plane in one interval.
Interval
How often the brush applies again while the button is held. It also applies once when the button is pressed.
The time in seconds between applications.
Linked: none (this part has no other layer that can be edited)
Step
How far the vertex at the brush's centre moves each interval. Vertices further out move less.
The distance in world units, up or down.
Radius
The size of the brush, shown by the brush sphere. Every vertex within it moves, less the further it is from the centre.
The distance in world units. If no vertex is inside the brush, only the nearest corner of the triangle under it moves.
Cursor Opacity
How solid the fill inside the cursor's wireframe is. Lower values let the collision under a large cursor show through.
0% shows only the wireframe; 100% fills the cursor solid.
Controls

The brush works while the mouse is over the viewport; holding the right or middle button flies the camera instead. The mode keys work while no mouse button is held. You can change them in the keybind and mousebind settings.

Edit
Create
Fall protection can only be generated for Elden Ring, Nightreign, Armored Core VI and The Duskbloods (Network Test).
Direction
Which outer edges get walls, by the direction they face in the world.

All edges, or only those facing one direction. North is +Z and east is +X, matching the direction the open world's map numbers increase. An edge faces away from its collision and counts for its nearest direction.
All
North (+Z)
East (+X)
South (-Z)
West (-X)
Drop Edges Only

When on, an outer edge gets a wall only if it borders standable ground (facing up, with slopes up to about 60 degrees) and, just past it, the ground of this part and the loaded collision parts around it is missing or lower than the minimum drop. Open seams between pieces of floor, and the edges of walls and ceilings, then get no walls. When off, every outer edge gets one.
How far below an edge the ground past it must be for the edge to count as a drop, in world units. Ground up to 0.5 above the edge also counts as ground.
Wall Height
How far the walls reach above the edges they stand on.
In world units. Every fall protection wall is 1.8 high in Elden Ring, Nightreign and The Duskbloods, and 10 high in Armored Core VI. Each game keeps its own height here.
Collision Filter
The collision filter info of the wall bodies.
The game's walls use 0 or 1. Elden Ring's legacy dungeons only use 1, and Armored Core VI's files usually hold one wall body of each. Copy the value of the map's other walls.

Map
The map the collision is made for: the map shown in the content tree, which follows the last selected object.
Collision Types
Which collision files to make at once. High and low hold the mesh; fall protection holds walls along the mesh's outer edges.
Make the high collision file (the mesh) in the map's high collision binder.
Make the low collision file (the same mesh) in the map's low collision binder.

Make the fall protection file in the map's fall protection binder: flat vertical walls along the mesh's outer edges, where the part places it in the world. Any existing walls of the model are replaced.

Shape
What the collision's mesh is.

A basic shape, placed at the placement orb; the FLVERs of the selected map pieces and assets, combined in place (the new part goes where the first of them in map order is); or User-Defined: a line, plane or box made from points placed in the viewport (the new part goes on the first point).
Made at the placement orb, {0} in front of the camera, currently at {1}. Move the camera to move it. Set the distance in the viewport's Settings > Placement Orb.

Square
Triangle
Circle
Semi-Circle
Selected FLVERs
User-Defined
Line
A vertical wall along the points, from each point up by the height.
Plane
The filled outline of the points. Each corner is at its point's height, so points placed on flat ground make a flat plane.
Box

The outline of the points, extruded into a closed solid, with the floor at the lowest point and the roof the set height above the highest. Two points make a rectangle along the world axes, with the points as opposite corners.
How the placed points become the collision's triangles.
Height
How far the wall reaches above each point.
How far the roof is above the highest point.
Closed Loop
Also join the last point to the first, so the wall goes all the way round. Needs 3 points.
Flip Facing
Turn the wall to face the other way. Without this, seen from above, the wall faces left of the direction the points were placed in. If you can walk through the wall in game, try the other side.
Up makes the faces point out of the box (the floor down, the roof up, the walls out). If you can walk into the box in game, try the other facing.
Points
The points the shape is made from, placed by raycast (clicking on what the viewport draws) or spawned and moved with the gizmo. Click a placed point's sphere to move it with the gizmo.
Raycast
Place each point by clicking in the viewport. It lands where the click meets the map.
Gizmo
Spawn points with Add Point and move each one with the gizmo. Points can go anywhere, including in the air or inside the map.
How points are placed. In either mode, you can move placed points with the gizmo by clicking their spheres.
How far along world X from the picked point (or the last point) a new point is spawned. The first point is spawned at the placement orb.
Add Point
Spawn a point after the picked point (or the last point), and pick it so the gizmo moves it.
Click in the viewport to add a point after the last one.
Place Points
Each click in the viewport adds a point where it lands on the map, until you stop placing.
Stop Placing
Stop adding points, so clicks select again.
Remove Last Point
Remove the point placed last.
Clear Points
Remove every point.

Facing
Which way the collision's faces point.
Up for standable ground. If you can fall through the collision in game, try the other facing.
Collision Material

The collision material of the triangles. A FLVER mesh whose material is named hkm_Name_Property keeps that material. The Material tab shows each face's material in its own colour, and paints new ones.
Parameters
The size of the shape, in world units.
Width
The size of the square along X.
Length
The size of the square along Z.
Size
The length of the triangle's sides.
Radius
The distance from the centre to the edge.
Segments
How many triangles make up the curve. More triangles make it smoother.
Source: {0} ({1})
Sources: {0} parts. The collision is placed where {1} is.
None of the selected parts' FLVERs could be read.
Couldn't read the FLVER of {0} ({1}), so it is left out.
Failed to read the FLVER of {0}.
Meshes
Which meshes of each FLVER go into the collision.
All
Use every mesh of every FLVER.
None
Use no meshes, to pick a few.
Simplify
A pass over the combined FLVER mesh that reduces its detail while keeping its overall shape, so the collision has far fewer triangles than the render mesh.
The mesh is simplified.
Simplify Mesh

Collapse the mesh's edges, cheapest first, until the target is reached or every further collapse would move the surface more than the max error. Flat areas reduce the most; slopes, steps and creases keep their shape.
Target
The share of triangles to keep. Fewer may be kept if the max error stops the pass first.
Max Error
How far, in metres, the simplified surface can stray from the original. Lower values keep more detail; higher values reduce further.
Keep Borders

Never move the vertices on the mesh's open edges or on borders between collision materials, so it still meets neighbouring collision exactly and each material keeps its area. When off, they can move, but at a heavy cost.
Simplified from {0} to {1} triangles ({2}%).
Model ID
The number of the new collision model. The part's model is h followed by this number, and its files are named after it.
Six digits. The suggestion is the first unused number after the map's highest number below 900000.
The model ID must be six digits.
The model ID must be in this game's format, like {0}.

In this game's format, like {0}. Demon's Souls and Dark Souls use four digits, B and a block digit (h1234B1, files h1234B1A10.hkx); Dark Souls II uses two digits, _ and four digits (h01_0200). The suggestion is the next free number in the block the map uses most.

Cleanup
Material
View and paint the collision material (the hit material: footstep sounds, effects, sliding and similar) of each face of the collision.

1. Choose the Layer (show it if it is hidden). While this tab is open, each face of that layer is drawn over the collision in its material's colour, and the Legend lists the materials shown with how many faces have each.
2. Select mode shows the clicked face's material, and you can type any hit material ID for it. To paint, choose the material by Surface (a HitMtrlParam row) and Property, from the Legend, or with Pick, which takes the clicked face's material.
3. Click Start Material Paint, then hold the left mouse button over the collision. With a Radius of 0, only the face under the cursor is painted. With a larger radius, every face of the layer within it is painted, limited by the Facing Limit to faces facing like the hit face.
4. Commit (above the tabs) rebuilds the repainted files and writes them into the project; Discard restores the materials.
Start Material Paint
While painting, clicking or dragging in the viewport gives the collision's faces the chosen material instead of selecting.
Stop Material Paint
Stop painting. Repainted faces are kept until you commit or discard them.

1. Find Unused lists the collision files of the active map that no part of its MSB uses. A part with model h001234 uses the h, l and f files ending _001234, whether the part is enabled or not.
2. Every listed file starts ticked; untick the ones to keep. Your choice is kept when you scan the same map again.
3. Cleanup removes the ticked files from the map's collision binders and writes the binders into the project immediately. This can't be undone.
4. The MSB as it is in the editor is what counts: if you delete a part and don't save the map, the game still has that part but no longer its collision. Save the map after a cleanup.
Files with uncommitted edits, files whose names don't follow the usual pattern, and a binder's last collision file are always kept.
Remove the collision files of the active map that no part uses.

Subtract
Cut a box out of the collision: what is inside it is removed, and triangles crossing it are cut along its faces.

1. Place the box: Place on Collision, then click the collision where it should be, or Place at Selection to put it on the selected object.
2. Move, turn and size it with the gizmo (its scale handles set the box's size) or with the Position, Rotation and Size fields. Rotation is in degrees about X, Y and Z.
3. Tick the layers to cut. A part's other layer is cut too when it is ticked, even if it isn't displayed.
4. Affected Collision lists the files the box reaches, with how many triangles it removes whole and how many it cuts.
5. Subtract cuts them, rebuilds the collision and writes the binders into the project. It can be undone.
Only visible collision parts are cut. Files with uncommitted Edit or Material changes must be committed or discarded first.
